# Philosophy Defined — OKF bundle

Cross-linked concept files for the Philosophy Defined archive. Each file
carries the page's full readable content; the `resource` field points at
the canonical HTML URL.

- [About Philosophy Defined | How the Archive Is Checked](about.md) — An archive of 696 philosophy quotations traced to their sources. 58 checked against a cited edition, with original wording and misattributions recorded.
- [Epistemology: Knowledge, Truth & Justification | Thinkers & Questions](branches--epistemology.md) — Epistemology explained: what knowledge is, when belief is justified, what scepticism can and cannot show, and the questions that define the theory of knowledge—with sourced passages.
- [Ethics: Moral Philosophy, Virtue & the Good | Thinkers & Questions](branches--ethics.md) — Ethics explained: what makes actions right, what a good life is, virtue and duty and consequence, and the questions of moral philosophy—with sourced passages from Plato to Murdoch.
- [Branches of Philosophy — Metaphysics, Ethics, Mind & More | Philosophy Defined](branches.md) — The 11 branches of philosophy, each explained with its central questions, key thinkers, and sourced passages: metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, logic, political philosophy, and the specialties.
- [Logic in Philosophy: Valid Reasoning & Its Limits | Thinkers](branches--logic.md) — Logic explained: validity, soundness, deduction and induction, the fallacies arguments actually commit, and why the study of good reasoning anchors every other branch—with sourced passages.
- [Metaphysics: What Exists, What Is Real | Key Thinkers & Questions](branches--metaphysics.md) — Metaphysics explained: what exists, what reality is made of, time, identity, and free will—its central questions and arguments, with sourced passages from the philosophers who worked on them.
- [Philosophy of Education: Learning, Teaching & Formation | Quotes](branches--philosophy-of-education.md) — Philosophy of education explained: what education is for, how learning forms a person, the examined life as a practice, and the arguments behind teaching—with sourced passages.
- [Philosophy of Language: Meaning, Reference & Truth | Thinkers](branches--philosophy-of-language.md) — Philosophy of language explained: how words mean, what reference is, where meaning lives — speaker, sentence, or world—and how language limits and enables thought, with sourced passages.
- [Philosophy of Law: Justice, Rights & Legal Obligation | Thinkers](branches--philosophy-of-law.md) — Philosophy of law explained: what makes law law, whether morality is part of it, why obedience is owed, and what rights and punishment are for—with sourced passages.
- [Philosophy of Mind: Consciousness & the Mind–Body Problem | Quotes](branches--philosophy-of-mind.md) — Philosophy of mind explained: the mind–body problem, consciousness and the hard problem, personal identity, and whether a machine could think—with sourced passages.
- [Philosophy of Religion: God, Faith & the Problem of Evil | Quotes](branches--philosophy-of-religion.md) — Philosophy of religion explained: arguments for and against God's existence, faith and reason, the problem of evil, and what the classical arguments actually claim—with sourced passages.
- [Philosophy of Science: Evidence, Explanation & Method | Thinkers](branches--philosophy-of-science.md) — Philosophy of science explained: what makes a theory scientific, how evidence confirms, what explanation is, and whether science describes reality—with sourced passages.
- [Political Philosophy: Justice, Power & the State | Thinkers & Quotes](branches--political-philosophy.md) — Political philosophy explained: justice, liberty, authority, and the legitimacy of the state—from Plato's city and Hobbes's Leviathan to Rawls—with sourced passages from each argument.
- [Branches of Philosophy | Philosophy Defined](branches-of-philosophy.md) — The main branches of philosophy explained: metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, logic, and political philosophy—with related specializations.
- [Chinese Philosophy | Confucianism, Daoism & the Way](chinese-philosophy.md) — Chinese philosophy explained: Confucianism, Daoism, Mohism, Legalism, and Buddhist thought—with verified English quotations and starter thinkers.
- [Confucianism vs Daoism | Philosophy Defined](confucianism-vs-daoism.md) — Confucianism vs Daoism: ritual and cultivation versus naturalness and the Way—compared without caricature.
- [Contact | Philosophy Defined](contact.md) — Report a quotation error, ask about a source record, or reach the editor of Philosophy Defined.
- [Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) | Philosophy Defined](doctor-of-philosophy.md) — What does Doctor of Philosophy mean? Learn what a PhD is, why the degree covers many disciplines, and what doctoral research involves.
- [Editorial Policy | Philosophy Defined](editorial-policy.md) — Our editorial policy for selecting, verifying, translating standards, and correcting English philosophy quotations.
- [a priori / a posteriori: from what is prior / from what is subsequent — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--a-priori-a-posteriori.md) — from what is prior / from what is subsequent. The distinction between knowledge that can be established without recourse to experience and knowledge that depends on it.
- [akrasia: acting against one's own better judgement — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--akrasia.md) — acting against one's own better judgement. Akrasia is the condition of knowingly doing what one believes one should not.
- [amor fati: love of fate — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--amor-fati.md) — love of fate. Nietzsche's formula for greatness in Ecce Homo: to want nothing different, neither forward nor backward nor in all eternity, and not merely to bear what is necessary but to love it.
- [anātman / anattā: not-self; the absence of a permanent self — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--anatman-anatta.md) — not-self; the absence of a permanent self. The Buddhist claim that no permanent, unchanging self can be found among the constituents of a person — body, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness — and that the belief in one is a source of suffering.
- [aporia: impasse; the state of being unable to proceed either way — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--aporia.md) — impasse; the state of being unable to proceed either way. Aporia is the condition a dialogue reaches when every answer offered has been refuted and none remains.
- [aretē: excellence, the fulfilment of a thing's own standard — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--arete.md) — excellence, the fulfilment of a thing's own standard. Aretē is the quality by which something does well what it is for — the aretē of a knife is a good edge, the aretē of a horse is running well, and the aretē of a human being is living as a human being should.
- [ataraxia: undisturbedness; freedom from disturbance — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--ataraxia.md) — undisturbedness; freedom from disturbance. Ataraxia is the goal of both Pyrrhonian scepticism and Epicureanism, reached by different routes.
- [ātman: self, breath, the innermost principle of a person — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--atman.md) — self, breath, the innermost principle of a person. In the Upaniṣads, ātman is the self that survives analysis — not the body, not the emotions, not the intellect, but that in virtue of which the other things are one's own.
- [brahman: the ground and totality of what is — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--brahman.md) — the ground and totality of what is. Brahman names the ultimate reality in the Upaniṣads — the source of the world, that from which things arise and into which they return, and the object of the knowledge the texts are meant to transmit.
- [cheng: sincerity, truthfulness, the completion of a thing's own nature — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--cheng.md) — sincerity, truthfulness, the completion of a thing's own nature. In the Zhongyong, cheng is at once a moral quality and a cosmological one: sincerity is the way of Heaven, and making oneself sincere is the human route to it.
- [conatus: striving; the effort to persist in being — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--conatus.md) — striving; the effort to persist in being. In Spinoza, conatus is the actual essence of a thing: each thing, so far as it can, strives to persevere in its being.
- [dao: way, path, course — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--dao.md) — way, path, course. In classical Chinese, dao is first a road and then, by extension, the course proper to something — the way a ruler governs, the way things proceed, the way to live.
- [de: virtue, power, the efficacy a thing has by being what it is — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--de.md) — virtue, power, the efficacy a thing has by being what it is. De is a thing's own power or potency, and in early Chinese thought it is closely tied to the idea that causing others to follow you is achieved through what you are rather than what you command.
- [dharma: the order that sustains things; also one's own duty; also a teaching — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--dharma.md) — the order that sustains things; also one's own duty; also a teaching. Dharma carries three senses that connect: the cosmic order that sustains the world, the specific duty that follows from one's position in that order, and — in Buddhism, where the Pali form is dhamma — the teaching and the constituent factors of experience.
- [elenchus: cross-examination; refutation by question and answer — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--elenchus.md) — cross-examination; refutation by question and answer. The elenchus is the method of Plato's early dialogues: Socrates asks what a term means, takes the answer offered, and by further questions draws the respondent into contradicting it.
- [epistēmē and doxa: knowledge and opinion — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--episteme-and-doxa.md) — knowledge and opinion. The distinction Plato draws in the Republic and the Theaetetus, and the one most of Western epistemology inherits.
- [epochē: suspension of judgement — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--epoche.md) — suspension of judgement. In Pyrrhonian scepticism, epochē is the withholding of assent that follows from the equal strength of opposing arguments — a practical discipline for reaching ataraxia, not a theoretical conclusion about our capacities.
- [esse and essentia: existence and essence — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--esse-and-essentia.md) — existence and essence. The distinction between that a thing is and what it is, which medieval philosophy inherits from Aristotle's distinction between existence and what-it-is-to-be and turns into a central question.
- [eudaimonia: living well and doing well; human flourishing — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--eudaimonia.md) — living well and doing well; human flourishing. Eudaimonia names the condition of a life going well taken as a whole, not a feeling at a moment.
- [habitus: a settled state; a durable disposition — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--habitus.md) — a settled state; a durable disposition. The Latin rendering of Aristotle's hexis: a stable condition of a thing that disposes it to act in a certain way, as distinct from a passing mood or a capacity one merely has.
- [ijtihād: exerting oneself to derive a ruling; independent legal reasoning — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--ijtihad.md) — exerting oneself to derive a ruling; independent legal reasoning. Ijtihād is the effort of a qualified jurist to reach a legal ruling on a question the received texts do not settle directly, by reasoning from the sources.
- [Glossary of philosophical terms | Philosophy Defined](glossary.md) — A working glossary of the technical terms in the archive's quotations — aretē, wu wei, śūnyatā, ressentiment — with the readings the sources do not support.
- [intellectus and ratio: intellective apprehension and discursive reason — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--intellectus-and-ratio.md) — intellective apprehension and discursive reason. The two modes of rational cognition distinguished in medieval philosophy.
- [junzi: the noble person, literally 'son of a lord' — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--junzi.md) — the noble person, literally 'son of a lord'. Junzi originally denoted hereditary rank: the son of a ruler.
- [karma: action, and the residue action leaves — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--karma.md) — action, and the residue action leaves. Karma names action and, by extension, the mechanism by which action shapes what comes next: a deed leaves a disposition, and the disposition tends to reproduce itself.
- [katharsis: purgation, cleansing — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--katharsis.md) — purgation, cleansing. Aristotle uses the word once, in the definition of tragedy in the Poetics, and says that tragedy effects through pity and fear the katharsis of those feelings.
- [li (principle 理) and li (ritual 禮): two entirely distinct concepts that English renders identically — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--li.md) — two entirely distinct concepts that English renders identically. A collision in transliteration that causes real confusion.
- [logos: account, reason, speech, proportion — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--logos.md) — account, reason, speech, proportion. Logos carries a family of senses that English splits across several words: the reasoned account one gives of something, the faculty that produces it, the speech in which it is delivered, and — in Heraclitus and the Stoics — the rational order of the world itself.
- [māyā: power of appearance; the tendency of the world to seem self-standing — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--maya.md) — power of appearance; the tendency of the world to seem self-standing. In Advaita Vedānta, māyā is the principle by which the single reality appears as many things, and by which that appearance is taken for what is real.
- [ming: mandate, decree, what is allotted — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--ming.md) — mandate, decree, what is allotted. Ming is the term for what is assigned to one and cannot be altered: the Zhongyong opens by saying that what Heaven mandates is called nature.
- [mu: the syllable of the first koan; no / nothing / without — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--mu.md) — the syllable of the first koan; no / nothing / without. The single-syllable reply Zhaozhou gave when asked whether a dog has Buddha-nature, and the subject of the first case of the Gateless Barrier.
- [niṣkāma karma: action without craving for its fruit — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--niskama-karma.md) — action without craving for its fruit. The Gītā's practical doctrine: act, and act fully, but do not let the action be motivated by its result.
- [nous: intellect; direct apprehension — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--nous.md) — intellect; direct apprehension. Nous is the faculty by which first principles are grasped, as distinct from the discursive reasoning that works out their consequences.
- [oikeiōsis: appropriation; coming to recognise something as one's own — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--oikeiosis.md) — appropriation; coming to recognise something as one's own. The Stoic account of how moral concern extends.
- [ordo amoris: the order of loves — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--ordo-amoris.md) — the order of loves. Augustine's account of virtue as rightly ordered love: a good will is one that loves things in proportion to their worth, God first, then creatures in their proper measure, and none of them as though it were the highest good.
- [phronēsis: practical wisdom; sound judgement about what to do — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--phronesis.md) — practical wisdom; sound judgement about what to do. Phronēsis is the intellectual virtue that governs action: the capacity to see what a situation calls for and to deliberate well about it.
- [prohairesis: the faculty of choice; what is up to us — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--prohairesis.md) — the faculty of choice; what is up to us. Prohairesis is Epictetus's central term: it names the power of choosing how to respond, and with it the whole of what he says is genuinely 'up to us'.
- [qi: the stuff and its dynamic configurations — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--qi.md) — the stuff and its dynamic configurations. Qi is what things are made of, so far as early and later Chinese cosmology makes that claim, but the concept is inseparable from its motion and its condensation: qi gathers and disperses, and a thing is a temporary configuration of it rather than a substance that possesses it.
- [ren: humaneness; being fully responsive to others as persons — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--ren.md) — humaneness; being fully responsive to others as persons. Ren is the central virtue of the Analects.
- [res cogitans / res extensa: thinking substance and extended substance — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--res-cogitans-res-extensa.md) — thinking substance and extended substance. The two kinds of substance Descartes argues for in the Meditations: mind, whose whole nature is to think, and body, whose whole nature is to occupy space.
- [satori: awakening; the direct seeing a practitioner works toward — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--satori.md) — awakening; the direct seeing a practitioner works toward. Satori is the Zen term for the experience of seeing one's own nature, and the tradition is careful that it is not a matter of acquiring information: the distinction between gradual cultivation and sudden awakening is a disagreement internal to Chan and Zen rather than between Zen and its rivals.
- [sub specie aeternitatis: under the aspect of eternity — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--sub-specie-aeternitatis.md) — under the aspect of eternity. Spinoza's phrase for the standpoint from which things are understood as following necessarily from the nature of God or substance, rather than as contingent events in a particular duration.
- [śūnyatā: emptiness; absence of own-being — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--sunyata.md) — emptiness; absence of own-being. In the Prajñāpāramitā literature and in Nāgārjuna's Madhyamaka, śūnyatā is the claim that things lack svabhāva — own-being, the intrinsic nature in virtue of which a thing would be what it is independently of anything else.
- [tawḥīd: affirming oneness; the unity of God — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--tawhid.md) — affirming oneness; the unity of God. Tawḥīd is the affirmation that God is one, without partner, and the term names both the doctrine and the act of affirming it.
- [telos: end, completion, the point of a thing — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--telos.md) — end, completion, the point of a thing. The telos of something is what its activity is directed toward, in the sense of what completes it rather than what merely stops it.
- [teshuvah: return; repentance — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--teshuvah.md) — return; repentance. Teshuvah means turning back or returning, and it names both the act of repentance and the state of being restored.
- [tikkun olam: repairing the world — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--tikkun-olam.md) — repairing the world. The phrase occurs in the Mishnah and in the prayer book with a narrower legal sense — enactments made 'for the good order of the world' — and was given a cosmological reading in Lurianic kabbalah, where it names the human task of gathering the sparks dispersed in the breaking of the vessels.
- [ubuntu: the quality of being a person; humaneness — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--ubuntu.md) — the quality of being a person; humaneness. Ubuntu is built on the stem -ntu with the class prefix for persons, and the maxim usually given for it is umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu — a person is a person through other persons.
- [vital force (force vitale): a putatively African concept of being as life-force — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--vital-force.md) — a putatively African concept of being as life-force. Prospero Tempels's Bantu Philosophy (1945) argued that the ontology underlying the Bantu languages treats being as force rather than as substance, with God as the source of a vitality that all things possess in different degrees.
- [wu wei: non-coercive action; acting without forcing — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--wu-wei.md) — non-coercive action; acting without forcing. Wu wei does not mean inactivity.
- [xin and xing: the heart-mind, and the nature one is born with — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--xin-and-xing.md) — the heart-mind, and the nature one is born with. Xin is conventionally translated 'heart-mind' because it covers both thought and feeling: the seat of intention, emotion, and cognition at once, and the thing a person has to rectify.
- [zhongyong: equilibrium and constancy; not the mean between extremes — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--zhongyong.md) — equilibrium and constancy; not the mean between extremes. Zhong names the state before joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure have been aroused — an equilibrium that is not itself a feeling — while yong names constancy or the steady application of the way.
- [ziran: self-so; what is so of itself — Meaning & Sources | Philosophy Defined](glossary--ziran.md) — self-so; what is so of itself. Ziran literally means 'so-of-itself' and was originally an adverbial pair, describing the way something is without an external cause rather than naming a domain of things.
